October 15, 2026

Bambu G-code This Week

This edition assumes nothing — every term gets explained as we go. Bambu's new A1-family firmware adds a bouncer at the door: it now decides which software is allowed to talk to your printer, and by default the answer is Bambu's own apps only. Two pieces of vocabulary first. The firmware is the software running inside the printer — it's what reads G-code and turns it into motor movements. G-code is the language of those instructions: plain-text lines like G1 X10 Y20 E0.5, each one telling the machine to move somewhere, extrude some plastic, set a temperature, and so on. Under the new firmware, third-party tools can still read the printer's status, but commands that do things — starting a print, moving the axes, running a calibration — get rejected unless they arrive through an authorized path. Bambu's authorized path is Bambu Connect: it works over your home network (LAN) with no internet connection and no Bambu account required. And tucked under LAN mode there's a Developer Mode that reopens the three channels hobbyists have always used — MQTT (a lightweight messaging protocol; think of it as the printer's text-message inbox for commands), FTP (plain file transfer, for sending print files), and the camera's live stream — turning the authorization checks off entirely.

Developer Mode restores most of the old behavior, but it comes with real tradeoffs: you lose Bambu Cloud access (no more starting prints from your phone when you're away from home), it's officially unsupported, and you have to enable it by hand on the printer's screen. I think this deserves an actual decision from you, because your whole setup leans local: your security bar runs higher than most, and a mode that keeps every command on your own network and drops the cloud handshake fits how you already work. Concretely, this is the switch that decides whether you'll ever be able to send raw G-code straight into the machine over MQTT — for example, driving the printer from your own scripts instead of Bambu's apps.

Meanwhile the current Bambu Studio betas are quietly changing the G-code they emit — the actual instructions your printer obeys. Vocabulary check: a slicer like Bambu Studio is the program that translates your 3D model into G-code. Every line it writes is a command the printer follows, so when the slicer changes, your prints change even if the model doesn't.

V2.8.4 trims travel moves on top-surface monotonic infill. Unpacking that: infill is the pattern printed inside your object — and on its visible top skin. Monotonic means every line of that pattern is drawn in the same direction, which makes top surfaces look smooth and uniform instead of patchy. A travel move is the nozzle moving without extruding plastic — just repositioning between lines. Travel moves print nothing, waste time, and can drag wisps of plastic across your surface, so fewer of them means faster, cleaner tops.

V2.8.3 adds three more. First, an Archimedean spiral ironing pattern. Ironing is a finishing pass where the hot nozzle glides over the top layer without extruding, melting it glass-smooth; the old pattern drew separate concentric rings, while the new spiral is one continuous outward path — you can see both in the image below, and you can read the difference directly in the G-code. Second, an independent first-layer infill line width: you can lay down extra-wide lines on layer one — wider lines grip the build plate better, so first layers stick more reliably — without changing the rest of the print. Third, a monotonic sub-top-surface infill: that's the layer hiding just beneath the visible top skin, and printing it monotonically gives the top skin a more even foundation to sit on.

V2.6.1 is smaller but useful: the G-code viewer — Studio's layer-by-layer preview of the actual instructions — now shows when the AUX fan runs. That's the auxiliary part-cooling fan on the side of the print head, the one that hardens fresh plastic on overhangs. It also doubles the A1 Mini's filament mapping from 16 to 32 slots. Filament mapping is how the slicer assigns each color or material in your project to a physical spool slot (for example, in an AMS unit); more slots means bigger multi-color projects without reshuffling spools. You can verify the travel-move change yourself, and it's a great first G-code exercise: slice the same plate in the old and new Studio, export both G-code files, and count the travel moves — lines starting with G0, the rapid-move command — in each. Fewer G0s in the new file, same model: that's the optimization, visible in the raw instructions. It closes the loop on the travel-ordering case study from the first briefing.

Two more worth your time. Extrudio renders photorealistic previews not from the 3D model but from the G-code itself, sweeping a virtual bead of plastic along the toolpaths. Toolpaths are the actual routes the nozzle travels — the G0 moves and G1 extrusion moves from your file. This is a deliberate mental reversal worth internalizing early: the model is what you intended, but the G-code is what the printer does. Any difference between the two — a slicer bug, a wrong setting, a firmware quirk — lives in the moves. That's also the exact math behind diagnosing under- and over-extrusion from code: compare how much plastic the G-code says to push (the E values on each line) against what the print actually needed, and the gap tells you which way your flow is off. And a community project rewriting the A1 Mini start routine (about 2,000 print hours of testing) documents how G380 guarded Z-moves and M1006 motor melodies work in practice. The start routine — also called start G-code — is the warm-up script your printer runs before every print: homing the axes, probing the bed, purging the nozzle. A guarded Z-move (G380) tells the printer to lower the nozzle until it feels resistance and stop — a touch-probe in a single command. M1006 plays melodies through the stepper motors themselves, vibrating them at audible frequencies like a tiny speaker. Study this project like a case file, not a recipe: custom start code runs with the nozzle hovering near the bed, so a wrong move means a real nozzle crash — anything you borrow gets a supervised first print.

One more, from the security corner of the same release notes: V2.8.4 fixes a stack buffer overflow in ADMesh's STL reader. In plain terms: when Studio opens an STL model file, a helper library reads it into a fixed-size chunk of memory called a buffer; the bug let a specially crafted file write past the end of that chunk — overflowing it — which can crash the program or, worse, be steered into running an attacker's code. File parsers are a classic attack surface because they chew on untrusted input, and this one sat in the tool you use every day. It's patched now; just update.

Read the moves as the truth, and treat the model as the intent.

I'll keep watching Bambu's release notes for what else shifts in emitted G-code and firmware behavior.

—Cantor
